title: Semisimplicity from a root cell and opposite-root identities
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and $\mathcal R=(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ a finite reduced root datum with a base $\Delta$, as in [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Assume $\Phi$ spans $M\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ and $\mathbf Z\Phi^\vee=M^\vee$. Put $T=D_k(M)$ and let $\Phi^+$ be the positive roots. Let $H$ be a $k$-group scheme which is smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], connected [def-weil-connected-scheme], separated (its diagonal is a closed immersion) and of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; affineness is not an assumption. Suppose there are immersed homomorphisms $j:T\to H$ and $x_\alpha:\mathbf G_{a,k}\to H$ for all roots, where immersion means isomorphism onto a locally closed subscheme and $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$. Suppose, for some orderings, multiplication
$$\prod_{\alpha\in-\Phi^+}\mathbf A^1_k\times T\times\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\mathbf A^1_k\longrightarrow H,\quad (a,t,b)\longmapsto\left(\prod x_\alpha(a_\alpha)\right)j(t)\left(\prod x_\alpha(b_\alpha)\right)$$
is an open immersion with dense image. With $\chi_\alpha(t)=t(e^\alpha)$ and $j\alpha^\vee$ the monomial cocharacter, assume on points over every commutative $k$-algebra that
$$j(t)x_\alpha(z)j(t)^{-1}=x_\alpha(\chi_\alpha(t)z),\qquad
x_\alpha(u)x_{-\alpha}(v)=x_{-\alpha}\left(\frac v{1+uv}\right)j\alpha^\vee(1+uv)x_\alpha\left(\frac u{1+uv}\right)$$
where the second identity is required when $1+uv$ is invertible. Suppose also that $n_\alpha=x_\alpha(1)x_{-\alpha}(-1)x_\alpha(1)$ satisfies $n_\alpha x_\alpha(z)n_\alpha^{-1}=x_{-\alpha}(-z)$. Then $H$ is affine and semisimple, $j$ identifies $T$ with a closed maximal torus, and the root datum of $(H,T)$ is the specified $\mathcal R$, with $x_\alpha(\mathbf G_a)$ the root subgroup labelled $\alpha$ and monomial coroot $\alpha^\vee$. Semisimple means having no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, where solvable means that the iterated commutator subgroup becomes trivial. Group schemes, full torus characters, roots and geometric coroots have the meanings of [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. There is no restriction on the characteristic of $k$; the zero datum is allowed.

source.place: Lemma 6.3.14, equation (6.3.5), and proof of Proposition 6.3.15, printed pp.227--229; field criterion extracted from the proof, with the Weyl representative written as the three-factor rank-one word Read online; local PDF WANTED. No Stacks tag states this group-theoretic input.

proof.text:
First let $q:H\to C$ be any homomorphism to a commutative group scheme. For each $\alpha$, choose $t\in T(k)$ with $c=\chi_\alpha(t)\ne1$. Such a point exists: in coordinates a nonzero integer exponent of $\alpha$ gives a nonconstant Laurent monomial on the infinite algebraically closed field. For every $k$-algebra and $z$ the given conjugation identity gives
$$x_\alpha(z)=[j(t),x_\alpha(z/(c-1))].$$
Hence $qx_\alpha=1$ as a scheme homomorphism. Put $u=1$, $v=s-1$ in the assumed opposite-root identity, for any unit $s$ in any test algebra. Applying $q$ gives $qj\alpha^\vee(s)=1$. Since the coroots generate $M^\vee$, the map from the product of their copies of $\mathbf G_m$ onto $T$ has a monomial section: choose an integer right inverse of the surjection from the free group on the coroots to the free lattice $M^\vee$. Thus $qj=1$. Consequently $q$ is trivial on the entire given open cell. These are identities of morphisms, not just identities on $k$-points.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.15, first paragraph of proof, printed p.228; equation (6.3.5), p.227

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-barsotti-chevalley-decomposition] to the smooth connected separated finite-type $k$-group $H$. It gives $L\hookrightarrow H$ affine and $p:H\to C$ with kernel $L$, where $C$ is an abelian variety, hence commutative and separated. Step 1 makes $p$ trivial on the dense open cell. The group $H$ is reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]. Therefore $p=1$ on $H$: the equalizer with the identity-valued morphism is closed by separatedness of $C$, and each section of its ideal vanishes on a dense open of a reduced scheme, so is zero. The scheme-theoretic kernel of $p$ is now all of $H$, so $L=H$. This proves affineness before using any theorem for affine algebraic groups.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.15, Chevalley argument, printed p.228; Milne Theorem 8.27, pp.154-155

proof.text:
Write $U_\alpha=x_\alpha(\mathbf G_a)$ and identify $T$ with its image. These are closed subgroup schemes: [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] factors each homomorphism through a closed image as the fppf quotient by its kernel; the assumed immersion has trivial kernel, so that quotient map is an isomorphism. At the identity, the open cell and [lem-sc-product-tangent-space-direct-sum] identify
$$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi} L_\alpha,\qquad L_\alpha=dx_\alpha(k).$$
Indeed on dual-number points the differential of multiplication is addition, so these are precisely the tangent inclusions of the displayed factors. Each $L_\alpha$ has dimension one. Differentiating the assumed conjugation formula in the root parameter, while retaining the whole torus as a group functor, makes $L_\alpha$ have character $\alpha$; $T$ acts trivially on its own tangent space. In particular the zero weight is exactly $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$, even when the differential of a root character is zero.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.15, tangent decomposition, printed pp.227-228; Stacks Tag 0BEB, varieties-lemma-tangent-space-product

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], $Z=C_H(T)$ is a smooth connected affine closed subgroup. By [lem-sfb-lie-normalizer-centralizer-invariants] and step 3, $\operatorname{Lie}(Z)=\mathfrak h^T=\operatorname{Lie}(T)$. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation] to the ambient group $Z$, the singleton family consisting of $T$, and the closed subgroup $T\subseteq Z$. Its tangent spanning hypothesis holds, so $Z=T$. Any torus containing $T$ is commutative and hence lies in $C_H(T)=T$; therefore $T$ is maximal. All centralizers here are scheme-theoretic, including on nonreduced test algebras.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.15, maximal-torus argument, printed p.228; Milne Proposition 10.34 and Theorem 17.38

proof.text: For each $\alpha\in\Phi$, reducedness of the specified root datum says that the positive rational ray through $\alpha$ contains no other root. Thus its positive-ray tangent subspace in $\mathfrak h$ is $L_\alpha$. Apply [lem-sfb-torus-positive-ray-subgroup] to the conjugation action of $T$ on $H$. The subgroup it constructs has tangent space $L_\alpha$; the two comparison implications in that statement, applied to the smooth connected $T$-stable closed subgroup $U_\alpha$, identify it with $U_\alpha$. In particular, if a smooth connected $T$-stable closed subgroup $K\subseteq H$ has $L_\alpha\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(K)$, then $U_\alpha\subseteq K$. This is the integration step needed below; mere inclusion of tangent spaces in positive characteristic would not suffice.

Let $U=R_u(H)$, supplied by [lem-sfb-unipotent-radical-existence]. The intersection $I=U\cap T$ is trivial. To see this scheme-theoretically, [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial] identifies smooth unipotence with an embedding into a unitriangular matrix group; restricting that embedding makes the closed subgroup $I$ unipotent. The inclusion $I\to T$ is then trivial by the same lemma. Since it is also a monomorphism, $I=1$. On dual numbers this gives $\operatorname{Lie}(U)\cap\operatorname{Lie}(T)=0$. Normality makes $\operatorname{Lie}(U)$ stable under $T$, so [lem-sfb-split-torus-representation-weight-decomposition] and step 3 show that if $U\ne1$, it contains some $L_\alpha$ in its Lie algebra. Here nontrivial smooth connected $U$ has positive dimension and nonzero tangent space: a zero-dimensional smooth connected group over an algebraically closed field is the identity. Step 5 now gives $U_\alpha\subseteq U$. Normality and the assumed $n_\alpha$ identity give $U_{-\alpha}\subseteq U$. Setting $u=1$, $v=s-1$ in the Gauss identity expresses $j\alpha^\vee(s)$ as a product of elements of these two root subgroups, so $j\alpha^\vee$ factors through $U\cap T=1$. This is impossible: $\alpha^\vee\ne0$ since $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ in the integer lattice, and its composite with $\chi_\alpha$ is the nonconstant scheme map $s\mapsto s^2$, also in characteristic two. Thus $U=1$ and $H$ is reductive.

source.place: Proposition 6.3.15, final paragraph, printed p.229; Milne Proposition 16.64 replaces the dynamic intersection calculation

proof.text: The torus character identification $X^*(T)=M$ is [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality]. Since $H$ is reductive and $T$ is maximal, [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] supplies its geometric root datum, whose roots are the nonzero full-torus weights of $\mathfrak h$. By step 3 these are exactly the specified $\Phi$. The uniqueness in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations], or equivalently step 5, identifies its $\alpha$-root subgroup with $U_\alpha$. Since $\Phi$ spans $M\otimes\mathbf Q$, [lem-sfb-semisimple-roots-span] proves that $H$ is semisimple in the precise solvable-normal-subgroup sense of the item. It remains to check equality of the coroots, rather than just equality of the roots.

source.place: Theorem 12.9, Theorem 21.11, and Proposition 21.48, printed pp.233-234,428-430,439

proof.text:
Fix $\alpha$. By [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections], the centralizer $H_\alpha$ of the largest subtorus in $\ker\alpha$ is reductive of semisimple rank one and contains $T$. Both $U_{\pm\alpha}$ lie in it, since that subtorus acts trivially in the given conjugation formulas. Apply [lem-sfb-split-rank-one-classification] to $(H_\alpha,T)$. It identifies this pair with a central split torus times one of $\operatorname{SL}_2,\operatorname{PGL}_2,\operatorname{GL}_2$, with the diagonal torus. Choose the orientation so that $\alpha$ is the ratio of the first diagonal entry to the second. The standard upper and lower unitriangular subgroups have weights $\pm\alpha$ and tangent spaces $L_{\pm\alpha}$, so step 5 identifies them with $U_{\pm\alpha}$. Consequently, in these coordinates,
$$x_\alpha(u)=I_2+auE_{12},\qquad x_{-\alpha}(v)=I_2+bvE_{21}$$
for $a,b\in k^\times$, where $E_{ij}$ is the matrix unit, with central coordinate $1$ and with matrix classes in the PGL case. The scalars follow simply because an automorphism of the affine line fixing zero is a degree-one polynomial, so a group-scheme automorphism of $\mathbf G_a$ over a field is scalar. In these models the geometric coroot $\gamma_\alpha^\vee(s)$ is $\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})$, with central coordinate $1$. Indeed the Weyl matrix $E_{12}-E_{21}$ swaps the two diagonal entries and fixes the central factor. For any torus character $\chi$ this gives $s_\alpha(\chi)=\chi-\langle\chi,\gamma_\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ by subtraction of its two matrix exponents. The uniqueness of the cocharacter satisfying this reflection identity in [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] identifies this explicit diagonal map with the geometric coroot.

source.place: Theorem 20.33, Corollary 20.34, and proof of Theorem 21.11, printed pp.418-419,429-430

proof.text:
In any of the three matrix models, direct multiplication of the two matrices in step 8, with $w_c=1+abuv$ invertible, gives
$$x_\alpha(u)x_{-\alpha}(v)=x_{-\alpha}(v/w_c)\gamma_\alpha^\vee(w_c)x_\alpha(u/w_c).$$
Compare this with the assumed formula, with $w=1+uv$. These are two factorizations of the same element in $U_{-\alpha}TU_\alpha$, so the original open-cell immersion forces equality of their factors: set every other root coordinate to zero in that immersion. This is the shape of the cell when $\alpha\in\Phi^+$. When $\alpha\in-\Phi^+$, compare instead the inverses of the two factorizations, $x_\alpha(-u/w)\,j\alpha^\vee(w)^{-1}x_{-\alpha}(-v/w)$ and $x_\alpha(-u/w_c)\,\gamma_\alpha^\vee(w_c)^{-1}x_{-\alpha}(-v/w_c)$, which lie in $U_\alpha TU_{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha$ negative and $-\alpha$ positive; there the positive-root parameters give $v/w=v/w_c$, hence $(ab-1)uv^2=0$, and the torus factors are compared through their inverses, with the same conclusions below. Work over $B=k[u,v,w^{-1},w_c^{-1}]$. Equality of the positive-root parameters yields $u/w=u/w_c$, hence $(ab-1)u^2v=0$ in this domain; therefore $ab=1$. Now both formulas hold with $w_c=w$ over every test algebra. Equality of the torus factors gives $j\alpha^\vee(1+uv)=\gamma_\alpha^\vee(1+uv)$. Setting $u=1$, $v=s-1$ over $k[s,s^{-1}]$ proves equality of the two cocharacters as scheme morphisms. This verifies every coroot, completing the root-datum identification. For $\Phi=\varnothing$, the spanning assumption gives $M=0$; the zero-weight calculation and step 4 already give $H=T=1$, so no rank-one argument is needed.
